    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27106v1</id>
    <title>Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T04:32:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27106v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27106v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models are increasingly used to extract records, generate SQL, summarize reports, answer policy questions, and route operational work. At these software boundaries, parseable output is necessary but does not establish task correctness. We present a reproducible benchmark protocol, a public executable artifact, and a confirmatory live API evaluation that separate structural validity from task-specific correctness across five business workflow tasks and six Python implementation conditions: PydanticAI, LangGraph, DSPy, CrewAI, Agno, and a framework-free SDK reference.
  We hypothesize that (H1) schema validity and task quality are separable, (H2) structured-output binding paths are heterogeneous under a shared model and lowest-common-denominator contract, and (H3) condition-by-task interactions concentrate failures rather than shifting all tasks equally. Confirmatory analysis uses distinct task instances (100 extraction and 50 per other task, with three nested replicates) under a frozen analysis plan, yielding a 5400-row primary matrix with equivalence margins and Holm-adjusted contrasts against the SDK reference.
  In the eligible confirmatory run, overall schema validity was 0.684 and mean automated quality was 0.638. PydanticAI, LangGraph, and DSPy retained near-ceiling schema validity with mean quality 0.91-0.94, while the plain SDK, Agno, and CrewAI conditions were substantially lower in this package and model configuration. Schema-valid rows still produced many task-score flags, especially in extraction and compliance QA, and quality residuals show strong condition-by-task interactions (including a workflow collapse for CrewAI). Labelled ablations address retry budgets and feature-using mechanisms; primary contrasts remain system-configuration findings, not causal attributions to marketed library features.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25809v1</id>
    <title>ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs for Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T09:31:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25809v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25809v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25562v1</id>
    <title>AZOWL AgentOps: Task-Scoped Governance for Deployed Agent Applications</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T06:06:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25562v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25562v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>AZOWL AgentOps provides shared governance for deploying agents and delegating work to them. Human and agent senders can exchange messages or explicitly delegate a business task. Accepted work has a stable identifier that links the sender's authority, the assigned runner, any required approval, and result evidence. The default enrolled customer PC profile is read-only. We compare AZOWL components with a configured LangGraph application in 28 synthetic runs across four paired pilots. Original AZOWL services checked work admission, recipient routing, and workflow prerequisites in isolated tests. The configured LangGraph application supplied business task and dispatch records in application code. Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and issued zero writes when an approved delivery address changed. AZOWL's scope gate, exercised as a component, requested approval again on the same task. A product probe reused one registered provider across two workflows and checked prerequisite enforcement for ticket-task submission. The paired protected writes, including ticket creation, used mock providers. Of two deployed PC inventory reads with verified receipts, we traced the 0.6.57 run from submission through runner pickup and tool execution to the receipt, with matching local and central artifact hashes. A separate deployed GRC audit followed an operator-driven ticket lifecycle on sample records.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25111v1</id>
    <title>DSFlow: A Neuro-Symbolic Data Workflow Agent with Statistical Diagnostic Guardrails</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T19:48:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25111v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25111v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Data science workflows often require tools that presume non-trivial technical knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) reduce this barrier, but a gap remains between flexible general-purpose agents and statistically controlled pipelines. We introduce DSFlow, a LangGraph-based neuro-symbolic data-agent platform that combines reusable, LLM-selected skills with deterministic diagnostic guardrails. Skills provide extensible task knowledge. Symbolic validation can accept a proposed method, request clarification or replanning, override an unsuitable method, or supply a safe fallback. Regression and clustering case studies illustrate how DSFlow uses diagnostic evidence to correct method choices and documents those decisions in auditable reports.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21259v1</id>
    <title>Evaluating Authorization and Trust Boundaries in Agentic Orchestration Frameworks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T15:33:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21259v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.21259v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, and multi-agent collaboration, introducing security risks at orchestration boundaries. These risks depend on how identities are represented, operations are authorized, and instructions or information propagate between components. We evaluate LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, and OpenClaw through twelve experiments mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications using a common LLM (gpt-4o-mini). The experiments cover prompt injection, unauthorized resource access and command execution, memory poisoning, and inter-agent trust and identity attacks. Adversarial inputs induced unauthorized tool invocation, while tool chaining, stale filesystem validation, encoded instructions, and inter-agent delegation exposed weaknesses in authorization across component boundaries. Memory poisoning showed that untrusted state can influence responses, a risk distinct from conventional access-control violations. In the evaluated protected configurations, explicit authorization, controlled capability assignment, filesystem containment, and execution safeguards prevented specific unauthorized operations. The findings emphasize preserving authorization and information-trust boundaries throughout agentic workflows rather than treating framework capabilities or model-level instructions as sufficient security guarantees.</summary>
